why.correct: The phosphate heads are polar and hydrophilic, so they face the water: the outer sheet's heads face the extracellular fluid and the inner sheet's heads face the cytoplasm.
options: The fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. They point inward and meet in the middle, forming the oily core, away from water.
Correct. The hydrophilic heads face the water on both sides of the membrane.
Cholesterol sits between phospholipids in the bilayer, but it is a separate molecule, not bonded to the tails.
Sugar chains are attached to some proteins and lipids on the outer surface only, and never to the hydrophobic tails.

why.correct: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the bilayer's hydrophobic core and crosses without any protein.
options: Sodium ions carry a charge and hold a shell of water molecules around them. Moving them into the oily core costs a great deal of energy, so the bare bilayer almost blocks them.
Glucose is large and polar. It barely crosses a bare bilayer; cells take it in through specific transport proteins.
Correct. Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes through the oily core on its own.
Potassium ions are charged, like sodium ions, so the hydrophobic core almost blocks them.

why.correct: Membrane proteins transport specific substances, act as enzymes, bind signals, anchor the cell and, as glycoproteins, carry identity markers.
options: Correct. Transport proteins give specific ions and molecules a way across the bilayer.
The oily core is made by the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids, not by proteins.
Correct. Some membrane proteins are enzymes that work right at the cell surface.
Correct. Glycoproteins carry sugar chains that are part of the glycocalyx and mark cell identity.
Genetic instructions are stored in the nucleus, not in the plasma membrane.

why.correct: Red blood cells hold about 25 times more potassium than plasma does. When their membranes tear, that potassium pours into the plasma in the tube, so the lab measures a falsely high value. The pink color is from the contents of the burst cells.
options: The fresh sample was normal, so his kidneys are handling potassium fine. The problem was in the tube, not in him.
Correct. Burst red cells released their potassium-rich cytoplasm into the plasma in the tube.
Potassium moving into cells would lower plasma potassium, not raise it.
Platelets do not release sodium in amounts that could do this, and lab machines measure sodium and potassium separately.

why.correct: The glycocalyx (glyco- = sugar, calyx = husk) is the coat of sugar chains attached to proteins and lipids on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
options: Correct. The glycocalyx is the sugar coat on the outside of the cell.
There is no fat layer under the membrane. The only lipid in the membrane is in the bilayer itself.
There is a protein framework under the membrane, but it is not the glycocalyx, and the glycocalyx is on the outside, never the inside.
Human cells have one plasma membrane, a single bilayer. The glycocalyx is sugar chains, not another bilayer.

why.correct: This is an integral protein. Its hydrophobic amino acids sit inside the oily core of the bilayer, so it comes out only when the bilayer itself is broken apart.
options: Sugar chains are attached to proteins, but they do not anchor a protein into the membrane. Its hydrophobic region does that.
A protein sitting loosely on a surface is a peripheral protein. Those are the ones that wash off with salt water.
Correct. An integral protein's hydrophobic region is held in the bilayer's core.
Membrane proteins are made of amino acids like every protein. What matters is which of those amino acids are hydrophobic.

why.correct: From outside in: the interstitial fluid bathes the cell; the glycocalyx is the sugar coat on the outer face; then come the hydrophilic heads of the outer sheet, the hydrophobic tails of both sheets meeting in the middle, the heads of the inner sheet, and finally the cytoplasm.
Glucose leaves the capillary into the interstitial fluid that bathes the cell, then crosses the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm.
options: Correct. Interstitial fluid lies between the capillary and the cells it supplies.
Intracellular fluid is inside the cell. Glucose reaches it only after crossing the plasma membrane, so it cannot come before the membrane.
Red blood cells stay in the blood. Their glycocalyx is not on the path from plasma to a tissue cell.
The nucleus is deep inside the cell, past the cytoplasm, not between the blood and the cell.

why.correct: Hydrophobic tails do not mix with water. They are excluded from it, which is exactly why they end up hidden in the middle of the bilayer.
options: This step is right. A bilayer forms when phospholipids are in water, as they are in your body.
This step is right. The polar heads are hydrophilic and interact with water.
This is the error. The tails are hydrophobic, so they are kept away from water, not drawn toward it.
This step is right. Tail to tail is the arrangement that shields every tail from water.
This step is right. The hydrophobic core is the barrier to charged particles.

why.correct: High sodium and low potassium is the pattern of extracellular fluid. Interstitial fluid is extracellular fluid.
options: Red cell cytoplasm is intracellular fluid. It is high in potassium and low in sodium, the reverse of this sample.
Correct. High sodium with low potassium marks extracellular fluid, and interstitial fluid is part of it.
Fluid inside a white blood cell is intracellular fluid, which has high potassium and low sodium.
Intracellular fluid in general has about 140 mmol/L potassium and only 10 to 15 mmol/L sodium.

why.correct: Extracellular fluid is all fluid outside cells. Its two main parts are interstitial fluid, which bathes the cells, and plasma, the fluid part of blood.
options: Correct. Plasma is outside the blood cells, so it is extracellular fluid.
Correct. Interstitial fluid fills the spaces between cells and is most of the extracellular fluid.
The fluid of the cytoplasm is intracellular fluid.
A red blood cell is a cell, so the fluid inside it is intracellular, even though the cell itself floats in plasma.
The nucleus is inside the cell, so its fluid is intracellular.

why.correct: Cholesterol wedges between phospholipids. At body temperature it restrains the tails, making the membrane less fluid and less leaky; at low temperature it stops the tails packing into a stiff sheet. The membrane stays about equally fluid over a range of temperatures.
options: Cholesterol is itself mostly nonpolar and makes the core less leaky, not more open to ions.
The sugar coat is the glycocalyx, made of sugar chains on proteins and lipids. Cholesterol is not part of it.
Glucose crosses through specific transport proteins, not through cholesterol.
Correct. Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity in both directions.

why.correct: The membrane is fluid: each phospholipid moves sideways and swaps places with its neighbors millions of times a second. That is the "fluid" in the fluid mosaic model.
options: This is true, but it supports the classmate's idea, since it describes a movement that almost never happens. It does not show that phospholipids move.
This is true, but it is about where sugars are, not about whether phospholipids move.
This is true, but it describes how firmly proteins are anchored in the bilayer, not whether lipids move.
Correct. Sideways drift within a sheet shows that phospholipids do not stay in one spot.

why.correct: Platelets gather at a break in a blood vessel and help seal it. With too few platelets, small cuts keep bleeding longer.
options: Correct. Platelets help seal breaks in blood vessels, so too few of them means slow-stopping bleeding.
Defending against infection is the job of white blood cells, and her white cell count is normal.
Oxygen is carried by red blood cells, and her red cell count is normal.
A low platelet count does not raise plasma potassium. Burst red cells in a sample can, but that is a different problem.

why.correct: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. They push out their nucleus as they mature.
options: White blood cells keep their nucleus and defend against infection; they do not carry oxygen.
Platelets have no nucleus, but they are cell fragments that help seal broken vessels, not oxygen carriers.
Correct. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and carry oxygen.
Plasma is the fluid part of blood, not a cell. It carries only a little dissolved oxygen compared with red blood cells.

why.correct: A living membrane holds transport proteins, each for one substance or a small family of them, and the cell can add or remove them. Adding proteins that carry sodium opens a path for sodium. That control is what makes the membrane selectively permeable; holes punched in plastic cannot change.
options: Phospholipids drift sideways but stay packed side by side. The bilayer does not open gaps for ions.
The oily core blocks charged particles such as sodium ions, whatever signal arrives. Ions cross through proteins.
Correct. By adding transport proteins, the cell changes what crosses its membrane.
The glycocalyx is sugar chains on the outer face. It does not carry sodium across the membrane.

why.correct: Burst cells release their intracellular fluid into the plasma in the tube, which gives a falsely high potassium result while the patient is unchanged.

variables.name: Potassium measured in the sample's plasma
variables.why: The red cells' cytoplasm is potassium-rich. Their torn membranes no longer separate it from the plasma, so potassium spills into the plasma.

variables.name: Potassium in the patient's own bloodstream
variables.why: The cells burst in the tube after it left the patient. Nothing changed in the patient's body.

variables.name: Number of intact red blood cells in the tube
variables.why: Each cell whose membrane tears is no longer an intact cell, so the count of whole red cells falls.

why.correct: A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane (cristae). The ATP-making protein complexes sit on that inner membrane.
options: The Golgi is a stack of flattened sacs with single membranes. It modifies and sorts proteins; it does not make ATP.
Correct. The mitochondrion's folded inner membrane holds the ATP-making machinery.
The smooth ER is a network of single-membrane tubes. It makes lipids and breaks down some drugs.
A lysosome is a single-membrane sac of digestive enzymes.

why.correct: Rough ER builds and folds proteins for export, and the Golgi packages them into vesicles bound for the surface. A cell full of both is a protein exporter, like the pancreas cells that make digestive enzymes.
options: Correct. Rough ER plus a large Golgi plus vesicles at the surface is the equipment of a protein-exporting cell.
Steroids are lipids made in the smooth ER. A steroid-making cell would be full of smooth ER, not rough ER.
Absorbing cells are marked by a brush border of microvilli, which this description does not mention.
Moving fluid across a surface is the job of cilia, which this description does not mention.

why.correct: Cilia and flagella have a core of nine microtubule pairs around two central ones, and each centriole is nine sets of three microtubules. Microvilli have an actin core, and intermediate filaments are their own kind of fiber.
options: Correct. A cilium's core is microtubules arranged as nine pairs around two.
Correct. A flagellum has the same microtubule core as a cilium, only longer.
Correct. Each centriole is a short cylinder of nine sets of three microtubules.
Microvilli have a core of actin microfilaments, which is why they do not beat.
Intermediate filaments are a separate, rope-like fiber of the cytoskeleton, not microtubules.

why.correct: Motor proteins such as kinesin and dynein carry vesicles and organelles by walking along microtubules. Without microtubules, those tracks are gone.
options: The brush border is made of microvilli, which have an actin core, not microtubules.
Correct. Microtubules are the tracks that motor proteins use to carry vesicles.
Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide inside peroxisomes. That does not depend on microtubule tracks.
Fuel oxidation happens on and inside the mitochondrion's inner membrane, not on microtubules.

why.correct: The smooth ER holds enzymes that break down alcohol and many drugs. Heavy drinking makes liver cells build more smooth ER with more of these enzymes, so some medicines are broken down faster.
options: Rough ER makes proteins for export and for membranes. It is not the main site of drug breakdown.
Lysosomes digest material in acid and recycle worn-out parts. They do not break down most drugs.
The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins. It does not break down drugs.
Correct. More smooth ER means more drug-breaking enzymes, so medicines wear off faster.

why.correct: Autophagy (auto- = self, -phagy = eating) is the controlled recycling of a cell's own worn-out organelles: they are wrapped in membrane, delivered to a lysosome and broken into reusable building blocks.
options: Correct. Autophagy is self-eating for recycling, and the cell survives it.
That describes autolysis, self-digestion when lysosomes break open, which destroys the cell.
Protein building is the ribosome's job and has nothing to do with digestion.
Mitochondria do divide on their own, but that is not autophagy.

why.correct: An exported protein is built by a bound ribosome, folded in the rough ER, carried by vesicle to the Golgi, modified and sorted there, then packaged into a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane and releases it outside the cell.
Lysosomal enzymes work best at about pH 4.5 to 5, the acidic interior of the lysosome. The cytosol is near pH 7.2, where they work poorly, so a small leak does little harm.
options: The cytosol is full of proteins, which is exactly why a large leak (autolysis) destroys the cell.
Correct. These enzymes need acid, and the cytosol is close to neutral.
Catalase is inside peroxisomes and breaks down hydrogen peroxide, not other enzymes.
Ribosomes are not built from leaked enzymes; they build proteins, they are not recycled from them.

why.correct: Peroxisome oxidations produce hydrogen peroxide, a reactive oxygen species. Catalase in the same peroxisome breaks it down to water and oxygen.
options: Correct. Hydrogen peroxide is the by-product that catalase destroys.
Catalase does not act on ATP, and ATP is not what it turns into water and oxygen.
Oxidizing a fatty acid does not produce glucose, and catalase does not act on glucose.
Calcium ions are stored by the smooth ER. They are not made by oxidizing fatty acids.

why.correct: Short, nonmoving projections with an actin core are microvilli. They multiply the surface area of the membrane, which speeds absorption.
options: Correct. An actin core and no movement identify microvilli.
Cilia are longer, have a microtubule core, and beat.
A flagellum is much longer, has a microtubule core, and whips to move the cell.
Microtubules are fibers inside the cell, not projections of its surface.

why.correct: The inside of a lysosome is acidic, at about pH 4.5 to 5. Its enzymes work in acid, not at neutral pH.
options: This step is right. Autophagy begins by wrapping the old organelle in membrane.
This step is right. The package delivers its contents to a lysosome by fusing with it.
This is the error. The lysosome's interior is acidic, and its enzymes need that acid.
This step is right. Lysosomal enzymes break proteins, lipids and nucleic acids into their building blocks.
This step is right. Recycling the parts is the point of autophagy.

why.correct: Cilia and the sperm flagellum share the same microtubule core moved by dynein motors. If that machinery fails, airway cilia cannot sweep out trapped microbes, and sperm cannot swim.
options: Microvilli do not move and do not clear the airways; a defect in them would not explain either problem.
A lysosomal enzyme defect causes material to build up inside cells. It does not stop cilia or sperm from moving.
Correct. One defect in the shared microtubule core stops both airway cilia and the sperm flagellum.
A general ribosome defect would affect protein building in every cell and would not single out cilia and sperm.

why.correct: Red blood cells make ATP by breaking down glucose in the cytosol, a process that uses no oxygen. That is why they do not use up the oxygen they carry.
options: Cells cannot take ATP from plasma in useful amounts; every cell makes its own. Red cells do make ATP.
Correct. Without mitochondria, red cells make ATP by breaking down glucose in the cytosol.
Lysosomes digest material; they do not make ATP. Mature red cells also lack lysosomes.
The rough ER builds proteins; it does not make ATP. Mature red cells also lack ER.

why.correct: The endomembrane system is the set of membranes linked by vesicle traffic: the membrane around the nucleus, the ER, the Golgi, vesicles, lysosomes and the plasma membrane.
options: Correct. The ER makes membrane and sends it onward by vesicle.
Correct. The Golgi receives vesicles from the ER and sends vesicles out.
Correct. Lysosomes receive their enzymes and membrane from the Golgi by vesicle.
Mitochondria have their own two membranes and divide on their own. They do not exchange membrane with the ER by vesicle.
Free ribosomes have no membrane at all, so they cannot be part of a membrane system.

why.correct: Energy is never created. Mitochondria oxidize fuel molecules from food and capture the energy stored in their bonds as ATP. Oxygen is needed for those oxidations, but it is not the energy source.
options: Oxygen is used in the reactions, but energy comes from the fuel's chemical bonds, and no energy is created.
Cells hold only a few seconds' worth of ATP; the body's energy reserves are fat and glycogen, not ATP in mitochondria.
Without fuel molecules, mitochondria have nothing to oxidize and make almost no ATP.
Correct. Mitochondria convert stored fuel energy into ATP; they do not create energy.

why.correct: Lysosomes depend on their acid interior. Lose the acid and digestion slows, so recycling falls and undigested material builds up.

variables.name: Activity of the lysosomal enzymes
variables.why: Lysosomal enzymes work best at about pH 4.5 to 5. As the interior drifts toward neutral, they work poorly.

variables.name: Recycling of worn-out organelles by autophagy
variables.why: Autophagy ends in lysosomal digestion. With weak enzymes, the wrapped organelles are not broken down.

variables.name: Amount of undigested material stored inside the cell
variables.why: Material keeps arriving at lysosomes but is no longer broken down, so it builds up.

why.correct: The cytosol (cyto- = cell, -sol = solution) is the fluid part of the cytoplasm: water with dissolved ions, nutrients and proteins, in which the organelles sit.
options: Correct. The cytosol is the cytoplasm minus its organelles.
The cytoplasm is the cytosol plus the organelles. The cytosol is only the fluid.
The fluid between cells is interstitial fluid, which is outside the plasma membrane.
The space inside the ER is separated from the cytosol by the ER membrane.

why.correct: A gap junction is a cluster of protein tunnels that link two cells' cytoplasm, so ions and small molecules pass straight through.
options: A tight junction seals the space between cells. It does not connect their interiors.
A desmosome rivets cells together. Fluid can pass around it, but nothing passes through it from cell to cell.
Correct. Gap junction tunnels connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells.
The glycocalyx is the sugar coat on the outside of a cell, not a junction.

why.correct: Desmosomes hold skin cells together against pulling and rubbing. When they fail, friction separates the cells and fluid fills the splits as blisters.
options: Gap junctions let ions pass between cells; they provide little strength, so their loss would not make cells separate.
Tight junctions seal the spaces between cells but are not what holds cells together against pulling.
Microvilli are surface folds that increase absorptive area; they are not junctions.
Correct. Loss of desmosomes lets cells pull apart under friction.

why.correct: Six connexins in each membrane form a connexon, and two docked connexons make one tunnel.
options: Correct. Connexins build the connexons of gap junctions.
Cadherins are the adhesion proteins that cross the gap in desmosomes.
Claudins are the strand proteins of tight junctions.
Actin makes microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, not junction tunnels.

why.correct: Tight junctions seal the spaces between lining cells. Loosen them, and fluid and ions can leak through the spaces instead of passing through the cells.
options: Pulling apart and blistering follows loss of desmosomes, which hold cells together. Tight junctions seal rather than rivet.
Ion sharing through tunnels is the job of gap junctions, which this toxin does not target.
Correct. Loosened seals let fluid and ions pass between the cells.
Microvilli have an actin core and are not held up by tight junctions.

why.correct: A desmosome has a plaque on each side anchoring intermediate filaments, with cadherins gripping across the gap. It is common where tissue is pulled, like skin and heart.
options: Correct. Intermediate filaments loop into the desmosome's plaques.
Correct. Cadherins reach across the gap and grip each other.
Sealing is the job of tight junctions. Fluid still passes around a desmosome.
Passing ions between cells is the job of gap junctions.
Correct. Skin and heart are under constant pulling, and desmosomes resist it.

why.correct: Gap junctions let the electrical signal spread from each heart cell to its neighbors. Blocked, the signal could no longer pass cell to cell, so the cells would lose their coordinated wave of contraction.
options: Holding the heart's cells together is the job of desmosomes, which are intact here.
Correct. Without gap junctions, the electrical signal cannot spread from cell to cell, so the contraction is no longer coordinated.
Sealing is the job of tight junctions, which are intact, and gap junctions do not seal.
Mitochondria make ATP inside each cell, which does not depend on gap junctions.

why.correct: The pull travels from the cell to its desmosome plaques, across the gap through the cadherins, into the neighbor's intermediate filaments, and on through the whole linked net, so no one cell takes all of it.
Six connexins make a ring with a pore, the connexon. Two docked connexons form one gap junction tunnel.
options: Correct. A connexon is the half-tunnel built from six connexins.
A desmosome is a riveting junction built from cadherins and plaques, not connexins.
A plaque is the dense protein pad inside a desmosome; it has no pore.
Tight junction strands are built from claudins and occludin and seal the gap rather than tunnel through it.

why.correct: Tight junctions form a continuous seal around each lining cell, so the space between cells is closed. A substance must cross the cells' own plasma membranes instead.
options: Desmosomes are spot welds; fluid and small molecules pass around them freely.
Gap junctions connect one lining cell to another. They do not draw substances in from the intestine.
Correct. The continuous seal of tight junctions closes the route between the cells.
Microvilli increase surface area for absorption. They do not trap substances or block the space between cells.

why.correct: A sharp rise in calcium ions (or a fall in pH) inside a cell closes its connexons. That is what stops ions passing and seals off the neighbors.
options: This step is right. The sequence begins with serious damage to one cell.
This step is right. Damaged cells take in calcium ions from the extracellular fluid, where calcium is far higher.
This is the error. High calcium closes connexons; it does not open them.
This step is right. Closed connexons stop the flow of ions.
This step is right. Closing the tunnels protects the healthy cells.

why.correct: A tight junction runs as an unbroken band around each cell. Being continuous is what lets it seal.
options: A desmosome is a small button-shaped spot, not a continuous seam.
Correct. The tight junction is a continuous band.
A gap junction is a cluster of tunnels at one spot.
A hemidesmosome is a spot that anchors a cell to the material beneath it.

why.correct: Connexins build gap junctions. A defective connexin blocks the flow of ions between neighboring cells, which these ear cells depend on.
options: Riveting is done by desmosomes, which use cadherins, not connexins.
Correct. Connexins make gap junction tunnels, which share ions between cells.
Sealing is done by tight junctions, which use claudins and occludin.
Anchoring to the layer below is done by hemidesmosomes, not by connexins.

why.correct: Gap junction tunnels pass water, ions and small molecules such as glucose, amino acids and ATP. Large molecules like proteins are too big.
options: Correct. Ions pass freely, which is how gap junctions carry electrical current.
Correct. Glucose is a small molecule that fits through the tunnel.
Correct. ATP is small enough to pass.
A protein is far too large for the tunnel's pore.
Correct. Water passes through the tunnels.

why.correct: Tight junctions seal but give little strength. Desmosomes provide the strength. With tight junctions intact and desmosomes gone, the sheet stays sealed but cannot resist pulling.
options: The tight junctions are intact, so the sheet does not leak, and without desmosomes it cannot resist pulling.
The seal holds, but resisting pulling depends on desmosomes, which are gone.
The seal holds, and sharing ions depends on gap junctions, which are not affected.
Correct. The seal survives, but the strength does not.

why.correct: Gap junctions couple cells electrically. More of them lets a signal spread faster and wider, so the uterine wall contracts as a unit.

variables.name: Flow of ions between neighboring uterine cells
variables.why: More gap junctions means more tunnels between the cells' cytoplasm, so more ions can pass from one to the next.

variables.name: How closely the cells contract together
variables.why: Ion flow carries the electrical change from cell to cell, so a signal in one cell spreads quickly to many, and they contract together.

variables.name: Seal between the cells against leaks
variables.why: Sealing is the job of tight junctions. Adding gap junctions does not change it.

why.correct: Desmosomes resist pulling, so they are most abundant in tissue under mechanical stress, such as skin.
options: Correct. Skin is constantly pulled and rubbed, and its cells are held by many desmosomes.
Red blood cells float separately in plasma and are not joined to each other at all.
Urine is a fluid, not a sheet of cells, so it has no junctions.
White blood cells must move freely through tissue, so they are not riveted to neighbors.

why.correct: Carbon dioxide is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the oily core of the bilayer and crosses straight through, down its concentration gradient.
options: Sodium ions carry a charge, so the oily core almost blocks them. They cross through ion channels.
Correct. Carbon dioxide is small and nonpolar and passes straight through the bilayer.
Glucose is large and polar. It crosses on carrier proteins by facilitated diffusion.
Chloride ions are charged, like sodium ions, and need ion channels to cross.

why.correct: Sterile water has almost no solutes, so it makes the plasma around the cells hypotonic. Water moves into the cells by osmosis, toward their trapped solutes, and they swell. Enough swelling tears them open: osmotic hemolysis.
options: Shrinking happens in a hypertonic solution, which has more nonpenetrating solutes than the cell. Water has fewer.
Cells keep their size in an isotonic solution, such as 0.9% sodium chloride, not in water.
Correct. The fluid around the cells is now hypotonic, so water enters and the cells swell.
Sterile water contains essentially no sodium, so there is none for the cells to take in.

why.correct: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the cell by osmosis. The cell shrinks (crenation, if extreme) and its solutes become more concentrated, but their number does not change.

variables.name: Volume of the cell
variables.why: The solution has more nonpenetrating solutes than the cell, so water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrinks.

variables.name: Concentration of solutes inside the cell
variables.why: Water leaves while the cell's solutes stay inside, so the same solutes sit in less water.

variables.name: Number of potassium ions inside the cell
variables.why: Osmosis moves water, not the trapped solutes. The cell keeps the same potassium ions, now in a smaller volume.

why.correct: At low glucose, most carriers are empty, so more glucose means more carriers loaded and faster uptake. At high glucose, nearly every carrier is already busy. Uptake has reached the transport maximum: carrier saturation.
options: Glucose is too large and polar to cross the bilayer in useful amounts at any concentration.
Raising outside glucose makes the inward gradient bigger, not reversed.
Correct. With nearly every carrier occupied, extra glucose cannot speed uptake.
Carriers are specific. A glucose carrier does not switch to other solutes when glucose is high.

why.correct: Millions of ions per second is channel speed, because ions stream through an open tunnel without binding tightly. The strong preference for potassium over sodium comes from the channel's narrow, selective stretch.
options: Correct. Speed and selectivity for one ion mark an ion channel.
Carriers bind and change shape each cycle, so they move hundreds to a few thousand molecules per second. A glucose carrier also does not move potassium.
Aquaporins pass water and are shaped so that ions cannot follow.
Glycoproteins in the glycocalyx carry sugar chains for identity. They do not form ion tunnels.

why.correct: Passive transport moves a substance down its gradient with no ATP spent by the cell. Simple diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and filtration all qualify.
options: Correct. This is simple diffusion.
Correct. This is osmosis through water channels.
Correct. This is facilitated diffusion by a carrier.
Correct. This is filtration. The pressure came from the heart, not from ATP spent by the capillary cells.
Moving a substance from low to high concentration is against its gradient and needs ATP, so it is not passive transport.

why.correct: Aquaporins speed water movement, but water also crosses the bare bilayer slowly. Osmosis still pulls water in, so the cell still swells, just more slowly.
options: Water crosses the phospholipid bilayer slowly even without aquaporins, so some still enters.
Correct. Blocking aquaporins slows osmosis but does not change its direction.
In a hypotonic solution, water moves into the cell. Aquaporins do not decide the direction.
Ions do not replace water. Their movement depends on ion channels, which this drug does not affect.

why.correct: A carrier binds glucose on one side, changes shape to expose it to the other side, releases it where glucose is less concentrated, then resets. It is never open all the way through.
In a hypotonic solution, water moves into the cell, toward the side with more solute particles. It does not move out.
options: This step is right. That is what makes a solution hypotonic to the cell.
This step is right. The cell's potassium, proteins and phosphates stay inside, so the difference in solute particles lasts.
This is the error. Water moves into the cell, toward its trapped solutes.
This step is right. Water entering increases the cell's volume.
This step is right. A tear from severe swelling is osmotic hemolysis.

why.correct: The solution matches the cells' osmolarity, but glycerol is a penetrating solute. It diffuses into the cells, adding to their solutes, and water follows by osmosis. The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic, so the cells swell and may burst.
options: That would be true if glycerol stayed outside. Because it crosses the membrane, it does not hold water outside the cells.
Shrinking requires more nonpenetrating solutes outside than inside. Glycerol does not stay outside.
The cells' potassium stays trapped inside; glycerol entering does not push it out. The volume changes because water follows the glycerol in.
Correct. Glycerol enters, water follows, and the cells swell: isosmotic but hypotonic.

why.correct: The trigger was physical pressure on the membrane. Channels that open when the membrane is stretched or pressed are mechanically gated.
options: Voltage-gated channels open when the voltage across the membrane changes. Here the first trigger was pressure.
Ligand-gated channels open when a specific molecule binds to them. No molecule was involved in the first step.
Correct. Physical deformation of the membrane opens mechanically gated channels.
Leak channels are open most of the time; they do not open in response to a trigger.

why.correct: A channel opened by the binding of a specific molecule is ligand-gated.
options: Mechanically gated channels open to stretch or pressure, not to a molecule binding.
Correct. Binding of a specific molecule opens it.
Aquaporins are water channels. They are not opened by a binding molecule and do not pass ions.
Voltage-gated channels open when the voltage across the membrane changes, not when a molecule binds.

why.correct: A carrier moves its cargo by changing shape: binding on one side shifts it into a form that exposes the binding site to the other side.
options: Correct. The shape change carries the binding site, with glucose on it, to the inside.
A continuous open tunnel describes a channel. A carrier is never open all the way through.
Facilitated diffusion uses no ATP. The glucose gradient supplies the energy.
Glucose is too large and polar to dissolve in the oily core. That is why it needs a carrier.

why.correct: At very high glucose, every carrier in both cells is busy, so each cell runs at its transport maximum. The maximum depends on how many carriers there are, so cell A, with twice as many, moves about twice as much.
options: At saturation the gradient no longer sets the rate. The number of carriers does.
Each carrier runs at about the same top speed. Cell B has fewer, so it is slower, not faster.
Correct. Twice the carriers gives about twice the transport maximum.
Saturated carriers keep working at their top rate. Uptake stops rising; it does not stop.

why.correct: Flow equals the pressure gradient divided by resistance. With the wall's resistance unchanged, raising the gradient from 30 to 45 mm Hg multiplies flow by 1.5. More fluid leaves into the tissue, which can show as swelling. In a real capillary, proteins held in the blood pull against the push, so the net rise is even larger; the capillary topic shows why.
options: A higher pressure inside pushes more fluid out, not less.
Filtration depends on the pressure gradient, and the gradient has risen.
Blood cells are too large to enter the gaps, so they stay in the blood; they do not plug the gaps.
Correct. The pressure gradient rose by half, so filtration rises by about half.

why.correct: Ions move through an open channel down their electrochemical gradient, which combines the concentration gradient and the charge difference across the membrane.
options: Correct. The concentration gradient is one part of the electrochemical gradient.
Correct. The electrical charge difference is the other part.
The trigger decides when the channel opens, not which way ions move once it is open.
Movement through a channel is passive. ATP does not power it or set its direction.

why.correct: Inside the cell, an enzyme attaches a phosphate group to glucose right away. Phosphorylated glucose no longer fits the carrier, so free glucose inside stays low and the gradient stays inward.
options: Correct. Phosphorylation removes free glucose inside, preserving the gradient.
Carriers work in both directions. Net movement follows the gradient, so if free glucose built up inside, it would leave again.
Aquaporins pass water only and do not carry glucose.
Facilitated diffusion uses no ATP to move glucose across; the gradient powers it.

why.correct: Crenation (crena = notch) is the spiky, shrunken shape a red blood cell takes when water leaves it in a hypertonic solution.
options: Swelling and bursting in a hypotonic solution is osmotic hemolysis.
Correct. Water leaves, and the cell shrinks and puckers.
In an isotonic solution the cell keeps its normal disc shape; that is not crenation.
A channel opened by stretch is a mechanically gated channel, which has nothing to do with crenation.

why.correct: 3% sodium chloride is hypertonic. It raises the nonpenetrating solutes in the fluid around the brain cells, so water leaves the cells by osmosis and they shrink, easing the swelling.
options: Water enters cells when the fluid around them is hypotonic. This fluid is hypertonic.
The question states that sodium and chloride stay mostly outside, which is why they hold water outside the cells.
0.9% sodium chloride is isotonic. 3% is more than three times as concentrated, so it is hypertonic.
Correct. A hypertonic fluid draws water out of the cells.

why.correct: Each cycle moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in, both against their gradients, using one ATP.
options: The numbers are reversed. Three sodium ions go out and two potassium ions come in.
The directions are reversed. The pump sends sodium out, where sodium is already high, and brings potassium in, where potassium is already high.
Correct. Three sodium out, two potassium in, per ATP.
The pump moves three and two, not one and one. That uneven exchange is why each cycle moves one net positive charge out.

why.correct: Potassium leaks out of cells all the time, and the sodium–potassium pump brings it back in. With many pumps blocked, potassium keeps leaking out but is not returned, so it builds up in the plasma.
options: Digoxin contains no potassium. It raises plasma potassium by blocking the pump.
Correct. Blocked pumps stop returning leaked potassium to the cells.
The pump moves potassium into cells, not out. Blocking it cannot make cells pump more potassium out.
Ions are not converted into other ions in the body. The change comes from where potassium sits, not from making new potassium.

why.correct: Stopping the pump lets sodium and potassium run down their gradients. The cell swells as sodium and water enter, and secondary active transport slows because the sodium gradient it spends is shrinking.

variables.name: Sodium concentration inside the cell
variables.why: Sodium keeps leaking in down its gradient, and the blocked pumps no longer send it back out.

variables.name: Potassium concentration inside the cell
variables.why: Potassium keeps leaking out, and the pumps no longer bring it back in.

variables.name: Cell volume
variables.why: Sodium builds up inside and is no longer effectively held outside. Water follows the extra solute into the cell by osmosis, and the cell swells.

variables.name: Glucose uptake by the symporter
variables.why: The symporter spends the sodium gradient. As sodium builds up inside, the gradient shrinks, so there is less energy to drag glucose in.

why.correct: In primary active transport, the carrier itself splits ATP to move a substance against its gradient. A calcium pump does exactly that.
options: Glucose moving down its gradient on a carrier is facilitated diffusion, which is passive.
A carrier that uses sodium's gradient to move glucose is secondary active transport. It splits no ATP itself.
Water moving through aquaporins is osmosis, which is passive.
Correct. The pump splits ATP directly to move calcium uphill.

why.correct: Sodium rushes into the cell down its steep electrochemical gradient, and the symporter couples that downhill movement to glucose's uphill movement. The sodium gradient itself was built by the sodium–potassium pump using ATP.
options: Correct. The sodium gradient powers the symporter; the pump built that gradient with ATP.
Glucose is moving against its gradient here, so its own gradient cannot supply the energy.
Heat is not a usable energy source for moving a solute across a membrane.
Fluid pressure drives filtration, not carrier transport of glucose into a cell.

why.correct: Every form of active transport depends on ATP. The pump uses it directly; symporters depend on the sodium gradient the pump builds; vesicle formation and fusion use ATP. Simple diffusion needs none.
options: Correct. The pump splits ATP with every cycle and stops at once.
Correct. The symporter slows and stops as the sodium gradient runs down without the pump.
Oxygen crosses by simple diffusion, powered by its own gradient, so it continues.
Correct. Forming vesicles from the plasma membrane uses ATP.
Correct. Moving vesicles and fusing them with the plasma membrane uses ATP.

why.correct: Sodium binds inside, ATP phosphorylates the pump, the shape change releases sodium outside, potassium binds outside, the phosphate comes off, and the pump returns to release potassium inside.
The shape change opens the pump toward the outside, so the sodium ions are released into the extracellular fluid, not back into the cytoplasm.
options: This step is right. The cycle starts with sodium binding on the inside.
This step is right. Phosphorylation by ATP powers the shape change.
This is the error. Sodium is released outside the cell; releasing it back inside would move nothing.
This step is right. The outward-facing pump picks up potassium from outside.
This step is right. Losing the phosphate returns the pump to its inward-facing shape, releasing potassium inside.

why.correct: The two ions move in opposite directions on one carrier, so it is antiport. Sodium moving in down its gradient powers calcium moving out against its gradient: secondary active transport.
options: In symport both substances move in the same direction. Here they move in opposite directions, and calcium is moving uphill, so it is not passive.
The carrier splits no ATP; it spends the sodium gradient, so it is not primary active transport.
Correct. Opposite directions on one carrier, powered by the sodium gradient.
A channel lets one ion move down its gradient. This carrier couples two ions and moves calcium against its gradient.

why.correct: Cells take up cholesterol-carrying particles by receptor-mediated endocytosis: surface proteins bind the particles and gather in coated pits that pinch off as vesicles. With those proteins defective, the particles stay in the blood. This is familial hypercholesterolemia.
options: Phagocytosis engulfs large particles such as bacteria and does not depend on these specific surface proteins.
Correct. Without working surface proteins, the specific uptake of cholesterol-carrying particles fails.
Exocytosis releases material from cells. The problem here is taking material in.
The particles are far too large to diffuse across the bilayer. They enter by endocytosis.

why.correct: Phagocytosis ("cell eating") is endocytosis of a large particle: the membrane extends around it and encloses it in a vesicle that fuses with a lysosome.
options: Pinocytosis takes in small droplets of fluid, not whole bacteria.
Correct. Engulfing a large particle is phagocytosis.
Exocytosis releases material from the cell; this cell is taking material in.
Secondary active transport moves single ions and molecules on carriers, not whole particles in vesicles.

why.correct: In exocytosis, the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, which opens the vesicle to the outside and releases its contents.
options: Correct. Fusion is the step that opens the vesicle to the outside.
Enzymes are large proteins. They leave in bulk inside vesicles, not one at a time through a pump.
Proteins are far too large and polar to cross the bilayer.
Folding the membrane around material and pinching it off is endocytosis, which brings material in.

why.correct: Each exocytosis adds the vesicle's membrane to the cell surface. Endocytosis pinches membrane back off, and the two balance, so the surface area stays about the same.
options: Fusion makes the vesicle membrane part of the plasma membrane, so it does add membrane.
A phospholipid bilayer does not dissolve in water; its tails are hydrophobic.
The cell's surface area stays about the same, so it is not growing with each release.
Correct. Endocytosis retrieves membrane as fast as exocytosis adds it.

why.correct: Intestinal lining cells take up glucose on a symporter that carries sodium in with it. Each glucose molecule pulls sodium into the cells, and water follows the absorbed solutes by osmosis.
options: Making the gut contents hypertonic would draw water into the gut, which is the opposite of what helps.
Blocking the pump would shrink the sodium gradient and slow the symporter, reducing absorption.
Glucose does not open aquaporins. Water follows the absorbed solutes by osmosis.
Correct. The sodium–glucose symporter brings sodium in with glucose, and water follows.

why.correct: These pumps split ATP to push hydrogen ions into the stomach against their gradient. Blocking them means fewer hydrogen ions reach the stomach, so it becomes less acidic. This is how proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid.
options: The pump is what puts hydrogen ions into the stomach. Blocking it lowers them.
Hydrogen ions are pumped uphill into the stomach. They do not diffuse there down a gradient in useful amounts.
Potassium ions are not acidic. Acid depends on hydrogen ions, which fall.
Correct. Fewer hydrogen ions are pumped into the stomach, so acid falls.

why.correct: Both are integral carrier proteins that bind their cargo and change shape. Only the pump splits ATP, moves its ions uphill, and moves net charge (three positive charges out, two in).
options: Correct. The pump moves both ions uphill; the glucose carrier moves glucose downhill.
Correct. The pump is an ATPase; facilitated diffusion uses no ATP.
Both are integral membrane proteins, so this does not distinguish them.
Both bind their cargo and change shape, so this does not distinguish them.
Correct. Each pump cycle moves one net positive charge out; glucose carries no charge.

why.correct: Pinocytosis ("cell drinking") is endocytosis in which the membrane dips inward and pinches off a small pocket of extracellular fluid with whatever solutes are in it.
options: Engulfing a large particle such as a bacterium is phagocytosis.
Correct. Pinocytosis takes in fluid and its dissolved solutes, without selecting them.
Releasing contents outside the cell is exocytosis.
Pumping hydrogen ions is primary active transport, not vesicle transport.

why.correct: A pump-blocked cell swells because sodium leaks in and water follows. With outside sodium matching the inside, sodium's concentration push is gone and only the electrical pull of the negative inside remains, so far less sodium enters and far less water follows.
options: Removing the concentration difference leaves only the electrical pull on sodium, so less sodium enters, not more.
Correct. With the concentration push gone, far less sodium leaks in, so far less water follows.
Swelling depends on sodium leaking in, which depends on the sodium gradient, not only on ATP.
The pumps prevent swelling; stopping them is what allows it. Here the smaller sodium leak limits it.

why.correct: Exocytosis (exo- = outside) is the release of a vesicle's contents when its membrane fuses with the plasma membrane. It is how cells secrete products.
options: Correct. Fusion and release outside is exocytosis.
Folding the membrane around material and pinching it in is endocytosis.
Using the sodium gradient to move glucose is secondary active transport by a symporter.
A pump splitting ATP to move ions is primary active transport.

why.correct: Guanine pairs with cytosine. A purine (guanine) pairs with a pyrimidine (cytosine), and the two line up to form three hydrogen bonds.
options: Adenine is a purine, like guanine. Two purines together would make a rung too wide for the helix, and they cannot line up hydrogen bonds. Adenine pairs with thymine.
Thymine is a pyrimidine, so the width would fit, but its hydrogen-bonding groups do not line up well with guanine's. Thymine pairs with adenine.
Correct. Guanine and cytosine form three hydrogen bonds and make a rung of standard width.
Two guanines are two purines: too wide for the helix, and their bonding groups do not match.

why.correct: Pair each base (G→C, A→T, T→A, T→A, C→G, A→T) to get CTAAGT. The strands are antiparallel, so the partner's 3′ end lies opposite the first strand's 5′ end: 3′-CTAAGT-5′.
options: Correct. The bases follow the pairing rule, and the ends are labeled in the opposite direction because DNA strands are antiparallel.
The bases are right, but the ends are labeled as if the strands ran the same way. DNA strands run in opposite directions.
This repeats the original sequence with the ends flipped. A partner strand has complementary bases, not the same ones.
DNA uses thymine, not the base written here as U. Paired with adenine, DNA always places thymine.

why.correct: Thymine pairs with adenine, so A = T = 22%, and A + T = 44%. That leaves 56% for G + C. Guanine pairs with cytosine, so G = C, and C = 56% ÷ 2 = 28%.
options: 22% is the thymine value, and also the adenine value, since A pairs with T. Cytosine pairs with guanine, not thymine.
56% is guanine and cytosine together. Split it in half, because every guanine has one cytosine partner.
Correct. A + T = 44%, G + C = 56%, and cytosine is half of that.
44% is adenine plus thymine together, not cytosine.

why.correct: DNA sits in the nucleus. White blood cells have nuclei; mature red blood cells and platelets do not. So although red cells far outnumber white cells, the DNA comes from the white cells.
options: Mature red blood cells are the most numerous cells in blood, but they have lost their nucleus, so they carry no chromosomes.
Correct. White blood cells are nucleated, so they hold the patient's chromosomes.
Platelets are cell fragments with no nucleus, so they contribute essentially no chromosomal DNA.
Plasma is the fluid part of blood, not a population of cells; it holds only traces of loose DNA fragments.

why.correct: The nucleus has a nuclear envelope pierced by nuclear pores, chromatin filling its interior, and one or more nucleoli. The Golgi apparatus and lysosomes are separate organelles in the cytoplasm.
options: Part of the nucleus. The nuclear envelope is its double-membrane boundary.
Part of the nucleus. The nucleolus is a dense region inside it where ribosome halves are assembled.
Part of the nucleus. Chromatin is the DNA with its packing proteins.
Not part of the nucleus. The Golgi apparatus is a stack of membrane sacs in the cytoplasm that modifies and sorts proteins.
Not part of the nucleus. Lysosomes are digestive vesicles in the cytoplasm.
Part of the nucleus. Nuclear pores are channels through the envelope.

why.correct: DNA first wraps around histone cores to form nucleosomes. The string of nucleosomes coils into a thicker chromatin fiber, which folds into loops. When a cell divides, the loops compact much further into a visible chromosome.
Copying doubles the DNA but not the chromosome count. Each of the 46 chromosomes now consists of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, so there are 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids.
options: This counts each chromatid as a separate chromosome. Sister chromatids stay joined, and together they are still one chromosome.
This is the cell before copying, when each chromosome is a single DNA molecule. Copying adds a second chromatid to each.
23 is the count in an egg or sperm cell, which carries one set. Your body cells carry two sets, 46 chromosomes.
Correct. 46 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids.

why.correct: Replication is semiconservative. Each new double helix keeps one old strand, which served as the template, and pairs it with one new strand. The old strands do not rejoin.
options: This step is right. Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases, which separates the strands without breaking either backbone.
This step is right. Free nucleotides pair with the template by the base-pairing rule.
This step is right. DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides with covalent bonds and proofreads as it goes.
This is the error. Each copy keeps one old strand and gains one new strand (semiconservative replication).

why.correct: Pairing places the right nucleotides, but something must join them with covalent bonds into a continuous strand. That is DNA polymerase's job.
options: Correct. DNA polymerase links each nucleotide to the growing strand and proofreads it.
Histones package double-stranded DNA after copying. They do not build new strands.
Helicase separates strands; it does not link nucleotides. Linking is done by DNA polymerase.
The nucleolus assembles ribosome halves. It plays no part in copying DNA.

why.correct: Heat separates the strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between paired bases. A G–C pair has three hydrogen bonds and an A–T pair has two, so the segment with the most G–C pairs holds its strands together most strongly and needs the most heat.
options: Only 30% G–C means mostly A–T pairs, with two hydrogen bonds each. This segment separates at a lower temperature.
45% G–C is more than some but less than the richest segment, so it separates before that one.
70% A–T means only 30% G–C. This is the same as the weakest segment and separates easily.
Correct. The most G–C pairs means the most hydrogen bonds holding the strands together.

why.correct: Each phosphate group in DNA's backbone carries a negative charge. Opposite charges attract, so the negative backbone clings to the positive histone surface.
options: The bases are tucked into the middle of the helix, paired with each other. The histones contact the outside of the helix, which is the backbone.
Correct. The attraction between opposite charges holds DNA on the histone core.
Deoxyribose is a polar sugar, and the backbone faces the watery nucleus. The binding comes from charge, not from avoiding water.
Histones package DNA without cutting it. Each chromosome stays one continuous DNA molecule.

why.correct: Pairs 1 to 22 are autosomes. The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes (XX or XY).
options: Correct. 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes.
23 is the total number of pairs, which includes the sex chromosomes.
One pair is the sex chromosomes, not the autosomes.
46 is the total number of chromosomes, not pairs of autosomes.

why.correct: Replication is semiconservative. Each old heavy strand serves as a template and keeps its place, paired with a new strand built from light nucleotides. Every daughter molecule is one heavy plus one light strand.
options: This would happen only if the old helix stayed intact and a whole new helix were built beside it. Instead, each copy keeps one old strand.
Old strands are not discarded. Every copy keeps one old heavy strand, so none can be entirely light after a single round.
The new strands are built from the light nucleotides now available, so the molecules cannot stay fully heavy.
Correct. One old strand plus one new strand in every molecule.

why.correct: Almost every cell with a nucleus carries the same genome, copied from the same first cell. Cells differ because each uses a different subset of genes.
options: Cells do not discard the genes they do not use. A liver cell still carries the genes for skin proteins.
Correct. Same DNA, different genes in use.
Both have 46 chromosomes. Chromosome number does not differ between body cell types.
Every copy of your DNA comes from the same original through accurate replication, so the sequences are the same apart from rare copying errors.

why.correct: A gene is a stretch of DNA whose sequence codes for a working product, usually a protein. One chromosome carries hundreds to thousands of genes.
options: A chromosome is one whole DNA molecule and carries many genes.
A nucleotide is one building block. A gene is a sequence of many nucleotides.
Correct. A gene is a coding segment of DNA.
A histone core is a protein spool for packing DNA, not a piece of genetic information.

variables.name: Amount of separated, single-stranded DNA exposed
variables.why: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs. With it blocked, the strands stay paired, so fewer bases are exposed.

variables.name: Amount of new DNA made
variables.why: DNA polymerase needs an exposed template strand to pair nucleotides against. No separated strands means no template, so little new DNA is made.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in the cell
variables.why: Chromosome number depends on how many DNA molecules there are. The existing 46 are not destroyed, and without copying none are added.

why.correct: Ribosome halves are assembled in the nucleolus and leave through the nuclear pores. With the pores blocked, they accumulate inside the nucleus.
options: Mitochondria are made in the cytoplasm by the division of existing mitochondria. They never pass through nuclear pores.
Lysosomes bud from the Golgi apparatus in the cytoplasm. They never enter or leave the nucleus.
Correct. Ribosome halves built in the nucleolus exit through the pores, so blocking them traps the halves inside.
Glucose is a small molecule used for fuel in the cytoplasm; nothing about the pores would trap it in the nucleus.

why.correct: RNA uses uracil where DNA uses thymine. Uracil pairs with adenine, just as thymine does.
options: Thymine is a DNA base. RNA has uracil in its place.
DNA is the double helix. RNA is a single strand, though it can fold back on itself.
Correct. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.
Deoxyribose is DNA's sugar. RNA's sugar is ribose, which has one more oxygen atom.

why.correct: RNA polymerase pairs RNA nucleotides with the template: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C. The mRNA is 5′-AUGCCG-3′, which begins with the start codon AUG.
options: The pairing is right, but this uses T. RNA has no thymine; it places U opposite A.
Correct. Complementary bases, with U opposite A and the ends running opposite to the template.
This copies the template's own bases, swapping T for U. The mRNA must be complementary to the template, not the same.
This repeats the template itself. An mRNA is built from complementary RNA bases.

why.correct: The anticodon pairs base by base with the codon: G with C, C with G, A with U. Written in the opposite direction, it is 3′-CGU-5′.
options: Correct. Each base pairs with its partner, and tRNA uses U.
tRNA is RNA, so it carries U, not T.
This is the codon itself. The anticodon must be complementary to the codon.
These bases are complementary but in the wrong order: the first base of the codon must pair with the base at the 3′ end of the anticodon.

why.correct: The ribosome starts at AUG, which adds methionine, then reads UUU (phenylalanine) and GGC (glycine). At UAA no tRNA fits, a release protein frees the chain, and no amino acid is added.
options: A stop codon is not an amino acid. It ends translation without adding anything.
The start codon AUG also codes for methionine, so the chain begins with methionine.
Correct. Three amino acids, then the chain is released at the stop codon.
AUG both starts translation and codes for methionine. The ribosome keeps reading until it reaches a stop codon.

why.correct: This is a silent mutation. The genetic code is redundant, and a change in the third base often leaves the amino acid the same. The ribosome still adds glycine, so the protein is identical.
options: A protein is cut short only if the new codon is a stop codon. GGU codes for glycine.
Every later codon changes only in a frameshift, when bases are added or deleted. A one-base substitution keeps the reading frame.
An amino acid swap is a missense mutation. Here the new codon names the same amino acid.
Correct. Same amino acid, same protein: a silent mutation.

why.correct: The code is read in groups of three from the start codon. Losing one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is misread. Losing a whole codon keeps the frame: the protein lacks one amino acid and the rest reads normally.
options: Correct. One base lost is a frameshift; three bases lost is an in-frame deletion.
Deleting a multiple of three bases leaves the reading frame intact, so only the three-base deletion keeps the rest of the protein normal.
This reverses the two. It is the loss of one base, not three, that throws off the triplet reading.
Redundancy lets some base substitutions go unnoticed. It cannot hide a lost base or a lost codon.

why.correct: The swapped amino acid makes the protein misfold in the ER. Misfolded protein is held back in the ER, where much of it clumps, so little moves on through the Golgi apparatus to be secreted. That explains both problems: low blood levels leave the lungs unprotected, and the trapped protein injures the liver cells.
options: If it were secreted at a normal level, his lungs would be protected and his liver cells would not be injured. Very little reaches the blood.
Correct. The misfolded protein is held in the ER instead of continuing along the secretory pathway.
The protein is made on ribosomes docked on the rough ER and enters the ER; it never goes into the nucleus. The mutation affects folding, not the pores.
The stem says transcription and translation run normally. The problem arises after translation, when the protein folds.

why.correct: RNA polymerase carries out transcription. With it blocked, no new mRNA is made. Existing mRNAs are broken down within hours, so protein production then collapses too, and the liver cells, which are exposed first and make proteins at a high rate, die.
options: Correct. Blocking RNA polymerase stops transcription directly.
Ribosomes keep reading the mRNA already present until it is broken down. Translation fails later, as a consequence.
DNA is copied by DNA polymerase, a different enzyme.
Exocytosis falls later, once there are no new proteins to ship. It is not the step the toxin blocks.

why.correct: The gene is transcribed and the RNA spliced in the nucleus. The finished mRNA exits through a pore. Translation begins in the cytosol, and the signal sequence sends the ribosome to the rough ER. The protein passes to the Golgi apparatus in transport vesicles and leaves the cell by exocytosis.
Translation reads mRNA, not DNA. tRNA anticodons pair with codons on the mRNA, on a ribosome in the cytoplasm, while the DNA stays in the nucleus.
options: This step is right. Translation starts at the AUG codon.
This is the error. Anticodons pair with mRNA codons; the DNA never leaves the nucleus.
This step is right. The rRNA of the large ribosome half forms the peptide bond.
This step is right. No tRNA matches a stop codon, so a release protein ends translation.

why.correct: Transcription, splicing and the addition of the cap and tail all happen in the nucleus. Only the finished mRNA leaves. Translation and the secretory pathway happen in the cytoplasm.
options: In the nucleus. The DNA template stays there.
In the nucleus. The spliceosome works on the RNA before it leaves.
Not in the nucleus. Ribosomes translate mRNA in the cytoplasm.
Not in the nucleus. The Golgi apparatus is in the cytoplasm.
In the nucleus. The cap and tail are added before the mRNA exits through a pore.

why.correct: Both cell types carry the same genome. Pancreas cells hold transcription factors that switch the enzyme's gene on, and skin cells do not, so only pancreas cells transcribe it.
options: Your body cells keep the whole genome. The gene is present in skin cells but switched off.
A mutation would affect the gene's sequence, not a whole cell type's pattern of use. The gene is normal in both.
Correct. Different transcription factors switch on different sets of genes.
Both cell types carry the same number of copies. The difference is in how much the gene is transcribed.

why.correct: Alternative splicing keeps or skips different exons, so one gene yields several mRNAs and several related proteins. Changes to proteins after translation add still more variety.
options: Correct. One gene, several spliced versions, several proteins.
The code is unambiguous: each codon names only one amino acid. Several codons can name the same amino acid, which is the reverse.
Replication copies the same genes. It creates no new proteins.
A polyribosome makes many copies of the same protein from one mRNA, not different proteins.

why.correct: This is a polyribosome. Each ribosome starts at the start codon and reads the whole message, so each builds a full copy of the same protein. It makes many copies quickly from one message.
options: Splicing happens in the nucleus before translation, and spliceosomes are not ribosomes.
Each ribosome reads the mRNA from start codon to stop codon and makes a complete chain.
The ribosomes all read the same codons in the same frame, so they make the same protein.
Correct. Many ribosomes, many copies of one protein.

why.correct: UGA is a stop codon. No tRNA pairs with it. A release protein binds instead and frees the finished polypeptide from the last tRNA.
options: No tRNA and no amino acid match a stop codon. That is what makes it a stop.
The ribosome does not reread the message. It lets go of the chain and comes apart.
Correct. A release protein ends translation at the stop codon.
RNA polymerase works on DNA in the nucleus. It plays no part in translation.

why.correct: The signal sequence docks the ribosome on the rough ER. Without it, the ribosome stays free and releases the finished enzyme into the cytosol, so it never enters the secretory pathway.
options: Secretion requires entry into the ER, which depends on the signal sequence. Without it, the enzyme cannot reach exocytosis.
Correct. No signal sequence, no ER entry: the enzyme stays in the cytosol.
Membrane proteins also enter through the ER, which needs the signal sequence.
Lysosome proteins also pass through the ER and Golgi apparatus first, which needs the signal sequence.

variables.name: Rate at which new polypeptides are made
variables.why: Ribosomes form the peptide bonds. With them blocked, no new amino acid chains are built.

variables.name: Amount of newly made enzyme arriving at the Golgi apparatus
variables.why: Proteins reach the Golgi apparatus only after being made on ribosomes docked on the rough ER. No new chains means none enter the ER, so fewer vesicles bring new enzyme to the Golgi.

variables.name: Number of genes in the nucleus
variables.why: The drug acts on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. The DNA in the nucleus, and so the genes, are untouched.

why.correct: 61 codons name amino acids and 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA).
options: 20 is the number of amino acids. Most amino acids have more than one codon.
64 is the total. Three of them are stop codons that name no amino acid.
3 is the number of stop codons.
Correct. 64 minus the 3 stop codons.

why.correct: UAG is a stop codon. This is a nonsense mutation. The ribosome stops at codon 10, releasing only the first nine amino acids, far too short to fold into the working protein.
options: That would be a missense mutation. UAG names no amino acid; it ends translation.
The protein ends 390 codons early, so it cannot be normal.
Correct. A nonsense mutation near the start gives a short, useless chain.
A stop codon ends translation. It cannot make the chain longer.

why.correct: S stands for synthesis: DNA synthesis. During S phase each chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids.
options: In G1 the cell grows and does its normal work. It has not yet copied its DNA.
Correct. DNA replication defines S phase.
In G2 the DNA has already been copied; the cell checks it and prepares to divide.
Metaphase is part of mitosis. The DNA was copied long before, in interphase.

why.correct: S phase doubles the DNA, so G2 holds 12 pg. Mitosis and cytokinesis split it evenly, so each daughter returns to 6 pg, the same as the parent in G1.
options: This skips S phase. The DNA doubles before division, so the daughters are not left with half.
Division splits the doubled DNA between two cells. Each daughter receives half of the 12 pg.
Correct. Doubled in S, then halved at division.
The DNA is replicated in S phase, so G2 holds twice the G1 amount.

why.correct: In anaphase the 46 pairs of sister chromatids separate, and each separated chromatid counts as a chromosome. The cell briefly holds 92 chromosomes, 46 moving to each end.
options: 23 is the count in an egg or sperm cell. Mitosis never halves the chromosome number.
46 is the count through metaphase, when sister chromatids are still joined. Once they separate, each is its own chromosome.
Correct. 46 chromatid pairs become 92 separate chromosomes.
This doubles the count twice. The DNA is replicated only once per cycle.

why.correct: Prophase condenses the chromosomes and builds the spindle. In metaphase they line up across the middle. In anaphase sister chromatids separate. In telophase new nuclei form. Cytokinesis finishes by pinching the cell in two.

The mitotic spindle is built from microtubules that must grow and shrink to capture and pull chromosomes. Frozen microtubules cannot attach and pull correctly, so the spindle checkpoint keeps sister chromatids together and holds the cell in mitosis, where many cells die.
options: The G1 checkpoint checks size, nutrients, signals and DNA damage. Microtubules are not needed to pass it.
DNA replication uses DNA polymerase and helicase, not microtubules.
The drug acts on dividing cells. It does not send them into G0, and cells already in G0 are largely unaffected.
Correct. The spindle cannot work, so the spindle checkpoint stops the cell in mitosis.

why.correct: The drug harms cells that are dividing. The lining of the mouth and the stem cells that make blood cells divide constantly, so they are hit hard. Most heart and brain cells have left the cycle and rest in G0, so they are largely spared.
options: Heart and brain cells carry the same genome as every other cell. The difference is whether they are dividing.
Correct. Fast-dividing normal cells are harmed; cells in G0 are spared.
The heart receives a large blood supply, so the drug reaches it. It spares heart cells because they are not dividing.
These are normal cells. They are harmed because, like tumor cells, they divide often.

why.correct: p53 senses DNA damage and responds by halting the cycle or, if the damage is too great, triggering apoptosis. Without p53, neither response happens, so the cell divides with its damaged DNA and its descendants inherit the resulting mutations. That is why TP53 is a tumor suppressor gene.
options: Halting at the G1 checkpoint in response to DNA damage depends on p53, which this cell lacks.
Damage-triggered apoptosis also depends on p53. Without it, the cell does not self-destruct.
Correct. With no p53, damaged cells keep dividing, and mutations pile up.
Leaving the cycle is not the default response to DNA damage. Without p53, the cell has no signal to stop.

why.correct: An oncogene is the mutated, overactive form of a normal gene that promotes division. A protein stuck "on" is a stuck accelerator.
options: A tumor suppressor gene restrains division. Its cancer-causing mutations remove function, not add it.
A cyclin is a normal cycle protein that activates a CDK. The mutation described turns a gene into something abnormal.
A checkpoint is a pause point in the cycle, not a gene.
Correct. A gain-of-function change in a division-promoting gene makes an oncogene.

why.correct: A tumor suppressor protein acts as a brake. One working copy of the gene usually makes enough brake, so both must be lost. An oncogene's product is an accelerator stuck on; the other, normal copy cannot switch it off, so one copy is enough.
options: Correct. Losing a brake takes both copies; a stuck accelerator needs only one.
Tumor suppressor genes such as TP53, RB1 and BRCA1 sit on autosomes, so a normal cell has two working copies of each.
Every gene is copied once in S phase. This does not distinguish the two groups.
Mutation rate is not the explanation. Any gene can be hit by a copying error; the difference lies in what the two kinds of protein do.

why.correct: In metaphase the chromosomes line up on the metaphase plate with sister chromatids still joined. They separate in anaphase, and the spindle checkpoint prevents that until every chromosome is attached.
options: This step is right. Prophase condenses the chromosomes and builds the spindle.
This is the error. Metaphase is when the chromosomes line up; separation is anaphase.
This step is right. Shortening kinetochore microtubules pull the chromatids apart in anaphase.
This step is right. Telophase rebuilds the two nuclei.

why.correct: Interphase runs G1, then S (DNA replication), then G2, followed by the mitotic phase.
options: G0 is a resting state outside the cycle, entered from G1. It is not a step between G1 and G2.
Prophase is the first phase of mitosis. It comes after G2.
Correct. S phase sits between G1 and G2.
Cytokinesis ends the mitotic phase. It comes last.

why.correct: Cytokinesis depends on a ring of actin and myosin tightening to form the cleavage furrow. Mitosis itself uses spindle microtubules, so it finishes, leaving two nuclei in one undivided cell.
options: Without the contractile ring, no cleavage furrow forms, so the cell does not split.
Correct. Mitosis completes, but cytokinesis fails.
Chromosomes are separated by spindle microtubules, which the drug does not affect.
The nuclei form normally in telophase. The problem is that the cytoplasm is not divided.

why.correct: Cells that can become any cell type of the body, but not the supporting tissues of pregnancy, are pluripotent. These are induced pluripotent stem cells.
options: Totipotent cells can also form the supporting tissues of pregnancy. Only the fertilized egg and its first few divisions are totipotent.
Correct. Any body cell type, but not the supporting tissues: pluripotent.
Multipotent cells are limited to one family of related cells, such as blood cells. Heart, liver and nerve-like cells span unrelated families.
Unipotent cells produce only one cell type.

why.correct: They make several related cell types within one family, the blood cells, so they are multipotent.
options: Totipotent cells can make every cell type plus the supporting tissues of pregnancy. Blood stem cells cannot make, say, liver cells.
Unipotent cells make only one type. These make many kinds of blood cell.
Correct. Several related types: multipotent.
Pluripotent cells can make every cell type of the body. Blood stem cells are limited to blood cells.

why.correct: Differentiation works through gene expression. Each cell holds a different mix of transcription factors, which switch on different genes. The proteins made from those genes build microvilli in one cell and digestive enzymes in the other. The genome is the same.
options: Differentiated cells keep their whole genome; unused genes are switched off, not removed. Induced pluripotent stem cells show that the genes are still there.
Both are somatic cells made by mitosis, so both carry 46 chromosomes.
Cells do not pick up genes from their neighbors. Both carry the genome they inherited from the stem cell.
Correct. Same genome, different genes switched on.

why.correct: Shrinking, DNA fragmentation and breakdown into membrane-wrapped pieces that are engulfed without harming the tissue are the signs of apoptosis, carried out by the cell's own caspase enzymes.
options: A cell killed by injury swells and bursts, spilling its contents and harming the tissue. This cell shrinks and stays wrapped.
Cytokinesis splits one living cell into two living cells. It does not fragment the DNA.
Correct. This is orderly, programmed cell death.
Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells to distant sites, not the death of a cell.

variables.name: Number of cells in the population
variables.why: Cell number is set by division minus death. Division is unchanged, and death by apoptosis has stopped, so the population grows.

variables.name: Number of cells carrying unrepaired DNA damage
variables.why: Cells with damage too great to repair are normally removed by apoptosis. They now survive and pass the damage to their descendants.

variables.name: Amount of DNA in each cell in G1
variables.why: Each cell still replicates its DNA once in S phase and splits it evenly at division, so a cell in G1 holds the same amount as before.

why.correct: Cancer cells have gathered several mutations. They divide without the usual signals, escape apoptosis, and in a malignant tumor can invade and spread by metastasis.
options: Typical. Overactive oncogenes and lost tumor suppressors make division independent of outside signals.
Typical. Most cancers need several mutations, gathered over many divisions.
Typical. Blocking the path to apoptosis lets damaged cells survive.
Typical. Spread to distant sites is metastasis, the defining danger of a malignant tumor.
Not typical. Normal cells stop dividing when crowded; cancer cells keep dividing and pile up.
Not typical. Cancer cells usually have failed checkpoints, not extra ones.

why.correct: A CDK is active only while bound to its cyclin. Normally the cell destroys the cyclin and the CDK falls silent. If the cyclin cannot be destroyed, the CDK stays bound and active, and the cell cannot leave mitosis normally.
options: Correct. The cyclin stays, so the CDK stays active.
CDKs are present throughout the cycle. Only the cyclin is destroyed each round.
A CDK is a kinase, a different protein from the cyclin. It does not change into one.
The CDK switches off only when its cyclin is destroyed, which the drug prevents.

why.correct: Somatic (somat- = body) cells are all body cells other than the line of cells that produces eggs and sperm. They divide by mitosis.
options: Many somatic cells divide throughout life, such as those lining the intestine. Stopping division is being in G0.
Correct. Every body cell except the egg- and sperm-producing line.
That describes stem cells.
Only a few cells, such as mature red blood cells, lose their nucleus.

why.correct: Glycolysis is a chain of enzyme reactions dissolved in the cytosol. It needs no organelle, which is why cells without mitochondria, such as mature red blood cells, can still run it.
options: The inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain, the last stage. Glycolysis happens before pyruvate ever reaches a mitochondrion.
The fluid inside the mitochondrion is where pyruvate is broken down and the citric acid cycle runs. Glycolysis comes first, outside the mitochondrion.
Correct. The glycolysis enzymes work in the cytosol.
The nucleus holds the DNA. No stage of glucose breakdown happens there.

why.correct: The citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain are in mitochondria, and a mature red blood cell has none. It can run only glycolysis, and it converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.
options: Correct. No mitochondria means no aerobic stages, whatever oxygen is present.
How tightly the red cell's protein binds oxygen is not the limit. Even with free oxygen inside, the cell has no electron transport chain to use it.
Glycolysis does not use oxygen, so oxygen neither turns it on nor off. It runs in cells with plenty of oxygen as well.
This gives a purpose, not a mechanism. The cell makes lactate because it lacks the organelle for the aerobic stages.
