why.correct: With the last complex blocked, electrons cannot pass to oxygen. The chain stops, NADH cannot give up its electrons, and the citric acid cycle stalls. NAD+ runs short, so cells convert pyruvate to lactate to regenerate it, and glycolysis becomes their only ATP source. Lactate pours into the blood even though oxygen is present.
options: Glycolysis does speed up, but because ATP falls, not because cyanide acts on its enzymes. Cyanide's target is the electron transport chain.
His blood carries plenty of oxygen. The problem is that his cells cannot use it.
Correct. The block stops NADH oxidation, and lactate production takes over the job of regenerating NAD+.
Pyruvate becomes lactate in the cytosol, not in the mitochondrion, and cyanide does not catalyze that reaction.

why.correct: Glucose is split first, in the cytosol. The pyruvate then enters the mitochondrion, where it loses a carbon and its acetyl group is broken down by the citric acid cycle. Only then do the loaded electron carriers feed the electron transport chain, which makes most of the ATP.

O2 is used only at the end of the electron transport chain. There each O2 accepts four electrons and four H+ and becomes two water molecules. The oxygen atoms in CO2 come from glucose and from water used in the citric acid cycle, not from the O2 you breathe.
options: This is the common mistake. CO2 is made in the citric acid cycle and as pyruvate loses a carbon, steps that take their oxygen atoms from glucose and water, not from O2.
Lactate is made from pyruvate in the cytosol, a step that uses no oxygen gas.
Pyruvate comes from splitting glucose. Glycolysis uses no O2, so the label cannot enter it.
Correct. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and ends up in water.

why.correct: Metabolic CO2 comes from the mitochondrial steps that take carbon atoms off fuel: one CO2 as each pyruvate loses a carbon, and two in each turn of the citric acid cycle. That is 6 CO2 per glucose, one for each of its carbon atoms.
options: Not a CO2 source. Glycolysis splits a six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvates, keeping all six carbons.
Releases CO2. The carbon removed from pyruvate leaves as CO2, leaving a two-carbon acetyl group.
Releases CO2. Each turn removes two carbons as CO2.
Not a CO2 source. The chain handles electrons and H+, not carbon, and its product is water.
Not a CO2 source. Pyruvate and lactate both have three carbons; the reaction only moves electrons from NADH onto pyruvate.

why.correct: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP and makes 4, for a net gain of 2. Converting pyruvate to lactate makes no ATP; it only regenerates NAD+.
options: Glycolysis does make 4 ATP, but it spends 2 in its early steps, so the net gain is 2.
Correct. A net 2 ATP from glycolysis, and none from the lactate step.
About 30–32 is the yield with oxygen, when pyruvate is broken down fully in the mitochondrion.
The lactate step makes no ATP, but glycolysis before it still nets 2.

why.correct: Most ATP comes from H+ flowing back across the inner membrane. One NADH pumps about 10 H+, and one ATP uses about 4, giving about 2.5 ATP per NADH. The shuttle that brings electrons from glycolysis's NADH into the mitochondrion differs between cells, and some H+ leaks back without making ATP. So the total varies around 30–32.
options: Every glucose molecule is identical: six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens.
Correct. Non-whole-number H+ ratios, different shuttles and variable leak make the yield a range.
Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose in every cell. The variation lies in the mitochondrial stages.
Glucose cannot become ATP directly. Its energy is captured step by step through the stages.

why.correct: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, at the end of the chain, and it becomes water. CO2 comes from the carbons of glucose, released earlier as pyruvate is broken down.
options: This step is right. Glycolysis runs in the cytosol and nets 2 ATP per glucose.
This step is right. Pyruvate breakdown and the citric acid cycle release the carbons as CO2.
This step is right. The electron carriers feed the chain.
This is the error. Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain and forms water, not CO2.

why.correct: Without oxygen the chain cannot take electrons, so the cell uses pyruvate as the electron acceptor. Pyruvate is reduced to lactate and NADH is oxidized back to NAD+.
options: With no oxygen at the end of the chain, electrons back up and the chain stops. It cannot take NADH's electrons.
Correct. Reducing pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD+.
The citric acid cycle depends on the chain to regenerate its NAD+, so it stops when oxygen is gone.
There is no oxygen in this cell. Lactate is the end product here.

why.correct: Cutting off oxygen stops the electron transport chain first. That stalls the citric acid cycle, so CO2 output and mitochondrial ATP fall. Glycolysis speeds up and pyruvate is diverted to lactate, but at 2 ATP per glucose it cannot replace what was lost for long.

variables.name: ATP made by the electron transport chain
variables.why: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. Without it, electrons back up, H+ pumping stops, and the H+ flow that makes ATP stops.

variables.name: Lactate production
variables.why: NADH can no longer give its electrons to the chain, so NAD+ runs short. Cells convert pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+.

variables.name: Rate of glycolysis
variables.why: Falling ATP speeds up glycolysis enzymes, and lactate production keeps supplying NAD+, so more glucose is split per second.

variables.name: CO2 production
variables.why: CO2 is released as pyruvate is broken down and in the citric acid cycle. Both stop when NADH cannot be oxidized, so less CO2 is made.

why.correct: Glycolysis needs NAD+ to accept electrons, and a cell holds only a little. Without oxygen, NADH cannot give its electrons to the chain. Passing them to pyruvate turns NADH back into NAD+, so glycolysis can keep netting 2 ATP per glucose.
options: Correct. The lactate step recycles NAD+.
Lactate is a three-carbon fuel molecule, not ATP. It can be turned back into pyruvate later.
The lactate step happens in the cytosol and keeps pyruvate there. It does not move anything into the mitochondrion.
Pyruvate and lactate both have three carbons; no CO2 is released. And CO2 does not drive the electron transport chain.

why.correct: Every glucose broken down aerobically releases 6 CO2 in the mitochondria. More fuel oxidized per minute means more CO2 made per minute, which diffuses into the blood and is breathed out.
options: CO2 output is tied to how much fuel is broken down. Faster aerobic respiration means more CO2.
CO2 production stops only if pyruvate breakdown and the citric acid cycle stop entirely.
It would fall only if fuel breakdown slowed, as when oxygen is cut off.
Correct. CO2 production rises with the rate of fuel breakdown.

why.correct: Lactate leaves muscle quickly. Heart muscle and other cells oxidize it, and the liver rebuilds glucose from it, so blood lactate is back to resting within an hour or so. Soreness that peaks one to two days later comes from small injuries inside the muscle and the repair that follows.
options: Lactate does not stay trapped. It returns to resting levels within an hour or so, long before the soreness peaks.
Correct. The timing rules out lactate; fiber damage and repair explain delayed soreness.
Hard exercise does raise lactate production. It is simply cleared long before the soreness appears.
Lactate can be turned back into pyruvate and oxidized, but CO2 diffuses out and is breathed away; it does not cause soreness days later.

why.correct: At the last complex of the chain, each O2 accepts four electrons and four H+ and becomes two water molecules. Removing electrons at the end is what keeps the chain moving.
options: Correct. Oxygen takes the electrons and becomes water.
NAD+ accepts electrons earlier, in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. As NADH it is a donor to the chain.
Pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH only when oxygen is missing, in the cytosol, becoming lactate. It is not part of the chain.
CO2 is fully oxidized carbon released in the citric acid cycle. It accepts no electrons in the chain.

why.correct: The citric acid cycle and electron transport chain run in mitochondria, and together they raise the yield from 2 ATP per glucose to about 30–32. A cell that works nonstop, like a heart cell, has many mitochondria and depends on these aerobic stages.
options: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol, not in mitochondria.
Cells hold only a small amount of ATP and rebuild it constantly. Mitochondria make ATP; they are not storage tanks.
Correct. More mitochondria mean more capacity for the high-yield aerobic stages.
Mitochondria break fuel down; they do not build glucose, and oxygen is not a raw material for glucose.

why.correct: The chain's energy is stored briefly as an H+ gradient. A leak lets that gradient run down without making ATP. The chain runs faster and uses more oxygen, but the energy leaves as heat instead of ATP.

variables.name: ATP made per glucose
variables.why: Much of the H+ now returns through the leak, so less of it passes through the enzyme that makes ATP. Each glucose yields fewer ATP.

variables.name: Oxygen used by the cell
variables.why: The H+ gradient keeps draining, so the chain keeps pumping and passing electrons to oxygen as fast as it can. With less ATP made per glucose, the cell also breaks down more fuel.

variables.name: Heat released by the cell
variables.why: Energy released by the chain that is not captured as ATP leaves as heat. H+ flowing back through the leak releases its energy as heat.

why.correct: Each reduced FAD gives about 1.5 ATP through the electron transport chain. 2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP.
options: 5 is what 2 NADH would give (2 × 2.5). Reduced FAD gives less, because its electrons enter the chain further along and pump fewer H+.
1.5 is the yield of one reduced FAD. The question asks for two.
Correct. 2 × 1.5 = 3.
4 uses 2 ATP per reduced FAD, the older whole-number value. Current measurements give about 1.5.
